fun_facts: Female blue marlin outgrow males so dramatically that almost every "grander" ever weighed, a fish over 1,000 pounds, has been female: adult males rarely reach even half that size, in a species where both sexes can live past 40 years.

A blue marlin caught at 1,245 pounds and 12 feet long turned out, when its otoliths were read, to be only about 20 years old -- it had spent those two decades as one of the fastest-growing bony fish in the ocean.
The bill isn't a spear. A blue marlin hunts by swimming into a school and slashing its bill sideways through it, stunning or maiming several fish at once rather than impaling any single one.

measures.label: Lower jaw fork length
measures.help: Tip of the lower jaw to the fork of the tail, measured in a straight line -- the standard billfish measurement.

vocabs.label: Sex
vocabs.help: Blue marlin cannot be sexed externally in the field; unknown is the normal answer.

vocabs.label: Condition at release
vocabs.help: Billfish tagging is normally done boat-side, leaving the fish in the water where possible.

not_taggable.reason: a fish in poor condition or bleeding is unlikely to survive release, so tagging it wastes the tag and the reward

must_release.reason: Atlantic blue marlin may legally be retained only by an angler holding a federal Highly Migratory Species permit landing a fish at or above a 99-inch lower jaw fork length minimum, counted against a national quota of just 250 marlin and spearfish landed per year; every blue marlin encountered in this tagging programme is released
